<信纸有火燎过的痕迹，而行文中字迹逐渐凌乱>

……到晚上，契丹人逐个领出关押人等，就地斩杀。
兄弟们合计一番，横竖一死，不如趁乱逃出，搏个生路。
临别涕零，唯心系家中老幼。身上粮饷合计二十两三钱，一分为五，异向而逃。
此信人手一封，若有一人逃脱，需凭信中所记，将信与粮饷送至各家亲眷。倘皆身死无归，务将此信毁之，不可祸及家人。

再记诸兄弟籍贯、亲属如下：
赵石，栾城，母李氏，弟赵铁。嘱弟照顾好家母。
周富贵，蔚州，已无亲眷。
李景行，滹沱荻花洲，父李阿公、嘱妻月娘再嫁。
斡特剌，潢水，嘱弟妹好好生活。
舍朗，狼河，嘱妻历托万顾己身。

此为我等绝笔信，愿能送抵至亲手中，万谢老天保佑。

景行不才，代诸兄弟书绝笔于此
en:
(The letter bears scorch marks along the edges, and the hand grows more and more unsteady as it goes on.)

...By nightfall, the Khitans began taking the prisoners out one by one and killing them on the spot.
The brothers put their heads together and decided that, since death awaited us either way, we might as well use the confusion to make a break for it and fight for a chance to live.
At parting, tears fell freely. Yet all our thoughts were with the old and the young at home. Between us, the pay and provisions we carried came to twenty liang and three qian, so we divided it into five shares and fled in different directions.
Each man carries a copy of this letter. If even one of us escapes, he must deliver the letters and the money to the families of the others. If none of us returns alive, then this letter must be destroyed, so that no harm comes to our kin.

I set down here once more the names and families of my brothers:
Zhao Shi, of Luancheng. His mother is Madam Li, and he has a younger brother, Zhao Tie. He asks that his brother take good care of their mother.
Zhou Fugui, of Weizhou. He has no family left.
Li Jingxing, of Silvereed Shoal on the Hutuo. His father is Elder Li. He asks that his wife, Yueniang, remarry.
Wo Tela, of the Huang River. He asks that his younger brother and sister live well and carry on.
She Lang, of the Wolf River. He asks that his wife, Li Tuo, take good care of herself.

This is our final letter. We only pray it may reach the hands of our loved ones. Ten thousand thanks, if Heaven should grant its protection.

I, Jingxing, unworthy though I am, write down these final words on behalf of my brothers.

zh:
【器用·二】

【砚】

殷十一赠栗冈砚
李白
殷侯三玄士，赠我栗冈砚。
洒染中山毫，光映吴门练。
天寒水不冻，日用心不倦。
携此临墨池，还如对君面。

石砚诗
杜甫
平公今诗伯，秀发吾所羡。
奉使三峡中，长啸得石砚。
巨璞禹凿余，异状君独见。
其滑乃波涛，其光或雷电。
联坳各尽墨，多水递隐见。
挥洒容数人，十手可对面。
公含起草姿，不远明光殿。
致于丹青地，知汝随顾盼。

唐秀才赠端州紫石砚以诗答之
刘禹锡
端州石砚人间重，赠我因知正草玄。
阙里庙堂空旧物，开方灶下岂天然。
玉蜍吐水霞光静，彩翰摇风绛锦鲜。
此日佣工记名姓，因君数到墨池前。

【棋】

烂柯石
孟郊
仙界一日内，人间千载穷。
双棋未遍局，万物皆为空。
樵客返归路，斧柯烂从风。
唯馀石桥在，犹自凌丹虹。

送国棋王逢
杜牧
玉子纹楸一路饶，最宜檐雨竹萧萧。
羸形暗去春泉长，拔势横来野火烧。
守道还如周柱史，鏖兵不羡霍嫖姚。
浮生七十更万日，与子期于局上销。

【书】

草书歌行
李白
少年上人号怀素，草书天下称独步。
墨池飞出北溟鱼，笔锋杀尽中山兔。
八月九月天气凉，酒徒词客满高堂。
笺麻素绢排数厢，宣州石砚墨色光。
吾师醉后倚绳床，须臾扫尽数千张。
飘风骤雨惊飒飒，落花飞雪何茫茫。
起来向壁不停手，一行数字大如斗。
怳怳如闻神鬼惊，时时只见龙蛇走。
左盘右蹙如惊电，状同楚汉相攻战。
湖南七郡凡几家，家家屏障书题遍。
王逸少，张伯英，古来几许浪得名。
张颠老死不足数，我师此义不师古。
古来万事贵天生，何必要公孙大娘浑脱舞。

怀素上人草书歌
窦冀
狂僧挥翰狂且逸，独任天机摧格律。
龙虎惭因点画生，雷霆却避锋铓疾。
鱼笺绢素岂不贵，只嫌局促儿童戏。
粉壁长廊数十间，兴来小豁胸襟气。
长幼集，贤豪至，枕糟藉麴犹半醉。
忽然绝叫三五声，满壁纵横千万字。
吴兴张老尔莫颠，叶县公孙我何谓。
如熊如罴不足比，如虺如蛇不足拟。
涵物为动鬼神泣，狂风入林花乱起。
殊形怪状不易说，就中惊燥尤枯绝。
边风杀气同惨烈，崩槎卧木争摧折。
塞草遥飞大漠霜，胡天乱下阴山雪。
偏看能事转新奇，郡守王公同赋诗。
枯藤劲铁愧三舍，骤雨寒猿惊一时。
此生绝艺人莫测，假此常为护持力。
连城之璧不可量，五百年知草圣当。
en:
【Implements · Part Two】

【Inkstone】

Yin Shiyi Presents a Chestnut Hill Inkstone
Li Bai
Lord Yin, a master of the profound, gave me this Chestnut Hill inkstone.
It moistens the Zhongshan hare's-hair brush, its sheen rivals Wu silk's gleam.
In coldest weather, the water never freezes; with daily use, the mind knows no fatigue.
Carrying this to the inkstone pool, it is as if I face you once again.

Poem on a Stone Inkstone
Du Fu
Lord Ping, now a master poet, your talent I deeply admire.
On a mission through the Three Gorges, a long cry brought this stone inkstone forth.
A massive jade remnant from Yu's chiseling, its strange form only you could see.
Its smoothness is like rolling waves, its glow like lightning's flash.
Linked hollows each hold their ink, water ebbs and flows, now hidden, now seen.
It allows several to write freely, ten hands could face it at once.
You possess the grace of a drafter, not far from the Bright Hall Palace.
Placed in this realm of painting and calligraphy, I know you follow with your gaze.

In Reply with a Poem to Scholar Tang's Gift of a Duanzhou Purple Stone Inkstone
Liu Yuxi
The Duanzhou stone inkstone prized by all, you gave it knowing I pursue the Way.
The old relics empty in the Queli temple hall, the square kiln's base—was it ever natural?
The jade toad spits water, rosy light serene; colored brushes stir the wind, crimson brocade fresh.
This day, hired hands record their names; because of you, I often come before the inkstone pool.

【Chess】

The Rotten Axe Handle Stone
Meng Jiao
A single day in the immortal realm, a thousand years in the mortal world pass by.
Before a game of chess is finished, all things under heaven turn to void.
The woodcutter returns along his path, his axe handle rotted, scattered by the wind.
Only the stone bridge remains, still arching over the crimson rainbow.

Seeing Off the National Chess Master Wang Feng
Du Mu
Jade pieces on a grained board, one move grants largesse, most fitting under eaves with rain and rustling bamboo.
A weak form fades, spring streams grow long; a sweeping advance comes raging like a wildfire.
Holding to the Way like Zhou's Historian; in fierce battle, I envy not Huo Qubing.
This floating life, seventy years and ten thousand days more, with you I'll spend them on the board.

【Calligraphy】

Song of Cursive Script
Li Bai
The young monk named Huaisu, in cursive script under heaven stands alone.
From the ink pool flies the North Sea fish; the brush tip slays all Zhongshan hares.
In eighth and ninth month, weather turns cool; drinkers and poets fill the lofty hall.
Paper and plain silk fill several chests; the Xuancheng inkstone's ink gleams dark.
My master, drunk, leans on his rope-bed, in moments sweeping clean thousands of sheets.
Whirling wind, sudden rain, startling and swift; falling blossoms, flying snow, how vast and vague!
Rising, facing the wall, his hand never stops, a line of characters large as dippers.
Dimly, as if hearing gods and ghosts gasp; constantly, only seeing dragons and snakes dart.
Left coiling, right constricting like startling lightning, resembling Chu and Han locked in battle.
The seven commanderies of Hunan—how many households? Every household's screen bears his inscribed lines.
Wang Xizhi, Zhang Zhi—since ancient times, how many have won fame in vain?
Old Zhang the Madman's death not worth counting; my master follows this principle, not antiquity.
Since ancient times, all things value natural genius; why must it be Gongsun Daniang's Hutuo dance?

Song of Monk Huaisu's Cursive Script
Dou Ji
The mad monk wields his brush, wild and free, alone entrusted to nature's workings, shattering rules.
Dragons and tigers ashamed, born from dots and strokes; thunder and lightning retreat before the swift, sharp tip.
Fish-scale paper, plain silk—are they not precious? Only嫌 cramped, a child's play.
Whitewashed walls, long corridors, several dozen rooms; when inspiration comes, a slight release of heart's breath.
Old and young gather, worthy and bold arrive, pillowed on dregs, leaning on yeast, still half-drunk.
Suddenly, three or five shouts pierce the air, the walls covered, crisscrossed, with ten thousand characters.
Old Zhang of Wuxing, don't you be mad; Gongsun of Yexian, what do I care?
Like a bear, like a brown bear—not enough for comparison; like a viper, like a snake—not fit for analogy.
Embracing things, they stir, making ghosts and spirits weep; fierce wind enters the grove, flowers wildly rise.
Strange shapes, bizarre forms, hard to describe; among them, startled and dry, especially withered and stark.
Border winds, killing air, equally grim and fierce; broken rafts, fallen trees, vie in being shattered.
Frontier grasses fly afar, desert frost; northern skies chaotically shed Yin Mountains' snow.
A sidelong glance reveals skill turning ever novel; Governor Lord Wang composes poems together.
Withered vines, strong iron, ashamed to keep their distance; sudden rain, cold gibbons, startled for a time.
In this life, his peerless art none can fathom; borrowing this, he often finds protective strength.
Jade worth many cities, beyond measure; after five hundred years, the Cursive Sage is known.

zh:
【虞书·舜典】

虞舜侧微，尧闻之聪明，将使嗣位，历试诸难，作《舜典》。
曰若稽古帝舜，曰重华协于帝。濬哲文明，温恭允塞，玄德升闻，乃命以位。慎徽五典，五典克从；纳于百揆，百揆时叙；宾于四门，四门穆穆；纳于大麓，烈风雷雨弗迷。帝曰：“格！汝舜。询事考言，乃言底可绩，三载。汝陟帝位。”
舜让于德，弗嗣。正月上日，受终于文祖。在璿玑玉衡，以齐七政。肆类于上帝，禋于六宗，望于山川，遍于群神。辑五瑞。既月乃日，觐四岳群牧，班瑞于群后。
岁二月，东巡守，至于岱宗，柴。望秩于山川，肆觐东后。协时月正日，同律度量衡。修五礼、五玉、三帛、二生、一死贽。如五器，卒乃复。五月南巡守，至于南岳，如岱礼。八月西巡守，至于西岳，如初。十有一月朔巡守，至于北岳，如西礼。归，格于艺祖，用特。五载一巡守，群后四朝。敷奏以言，明试以功，车服以庸。
肇十有二州，封十有二山，浚川。
象以典刑，流宥五刑，鞭作官刑，扑作教刑，金作赎刑。眚灾肆赦，怙终贼刑。钦哉，钦哉，惟刑之恤哉！
流共工于幽州，放欢兜于崇山，窜三苗于三危，殛鲧于羽山，四罪而天下咸服。
二十有八载，帝乃殂落。百姓如丧考妣，三载，四海遏密八音。
月正元日，舜格于文祖，询于四岳，辟四门，明四目，达四聪。“咨，十有二牧！”曰，“食哉惟时！柔远能迩，惇德允元，而难任人，蛮夷率服。”
舜曰：“咨，四岳！有能奋庸熙帝之载，使宅百揆亮采，惠畴？”佥曰：“伯禹作司空。”帝曰：“俞，咨！禹，汝平水土，惟时懋哉！”禹拜稽首，让于稷、契暨皋陶。帝曰：“俞，汝往哉！”
帝曰：“弃，黎民阻饥，汝后稷，播时百谷。”
帝曰：“契，百姓不亲，五品不逊。汝作司徒，敬敷五教，在宽。”
帝曰：“皋陶，蛮夷猾夏，寇贼奸宄。汝作士，五刑有服，五服三就。五流有宅，五宅三居。惟明克允！”
帝曰：“畴若予工？”佥曰：“垂哉！”帝曰：“俞，咨！垂，汝共工。”垂拜稽首，让于殳斨暨伯与。”帝曰：“俞，往哉！汝谐。”
帝曰：“畴若予上下草木鸟兽？”佥曰：“益哉！”帝曰：“俞，咨！益，汝作朕虞。”益拜稽首，让于朱虎、熊罴。帝曰：“俞，往哉！汝谐。”
帝曰：“咨！四岳，有能典朕三礼？’佥曰：“伯夷！”帝曰：“俞，咨！伯，汝作秩宗。夙夜惟寅，直哉惟清。”伯拜稽首，让于夔、龙。帝曰：“俞，往，钦哉！”
帝曰：“夔！命汝典乐，教胄子，直而温，宽而栗，刚而无虐，简而无傲。诗言志，歌永言，声依永，律和声。八音克谐，无相夺伦，神人以和。”夔曰：“於！予击石拊石，百兽率舞。”
帝曰：“龙，朕塈谗说殄行，震惊联师。命汝作纳言，夙夜出纳朕命，惟允！”
帝曰：“咨！汝二十有二人，钦哉！惟时亮天功。”三载考绩，三考，黜陟幽明，庶绩咸熙。分北三苗。
舜生三十征，庸三十，在位五十载，陟方乃死。
……
en:
【Book of Yu · Canon of Shun】

When Yu Shun lived in obscurity and humility, Yao, hearing of his wisdom and intelligence, was about to have him succeed to the throne. He tested him through various hardships, and thus was composed the "Canon of Shun."
Examining into antiquity, we find that Emperor Shun, called Magnificent Splendor, harmonized with the emperor [Yao]. Profoundly wise, refined, and intelligent;温和恭敬，诚信笃实—his dark virtue was heard on high, and he was appointed to office. Carefully he displayed the five cardinal duties, and they came to be universally observed; he was placed in the general administration of affairs, and all was duly ordered; he received guests at the four gates, and all was harmonious; he was sent into the great wilderness, and amidst violent winds, thunder, and rain, he did not go astray. The emperor said, "Come, Shun! I have consulted you on affairs and examined your words; your words have proved effective in practice for three years. Ascend the imperial throne."
Shun yielded to [the emperor's] virtue and would not succeed. On the first day of the first month, he received the abdication in the temple of the Ancestor of Culture. He examined the pearl-adorned armillary sphere and the jade transverse tube, to regulate the seven celestial bodies. Then he made special sacrifice to God, offered burnt offerings to the six honored ones, gazed toward the mountains and rivers, and paid homage to all the spirits. He gathered the five jade tokens of rank. After the month, on a chosen day, he gave audience to the four mountain chiefs and all the shepherds, and returned the tokens to the various lords.
In the second month of the year, he made a tour of inspection eastward, reaching Mount Tai, where he offered a burnt sacrifice. He paid due homage to the mountains and rivers, and then gave audience to the eastern lords. He harmonized the seasons and months, and rectified the days; he unified the standard measures of length, capacity, and weight. He cultivated the five rituals, the five jade tokens, the three silks, the two living gifts, and the one dead gift. As for the five instruments, when finished, he restored them. In the fifth month, he made a tour southward, reaching the southern mountain, and performed the same rites as at Mount Tai. In the eighth month, he made a tour westward, reaching the western mountain, and performed the rites as at the beginning. In the eleventh month, he made a tour northward, reaching the northern mountain, and performed the rites as in the west. On his return, he went to the temple of the Ancestor of Culture and offered a single bullock. Every five years there was one tour of inspection, and the various lords paid court four times. They presented their reports in words, and were clearly tested by their achievements; they were given carriages and robes according to their merit.
He established twelve provinces, and raised altars to the twelve mountains, and deepened the rivers.
He made the statutory punishments emblematic [on garments]; banishment was a mitigation of the five punishments; the whip was used as the punishment for officials; the cane as the punishment for teachers; and fines as punishment for [minor] offenses. Inadvertent offenses were pardoned, but those who persisted in wrongdoing were punished with death. Be reverent, be reverent! Let compassion be shown in the use of punishments!
He banished Gong Gong to Youzhou, exiled Huan Dou to Chong Mountain, drove the San Miao to Sanwei, and imprisoned Gun on Yu Mountain. These four criminals being dealt with, all under heaven submitted.
After twenty-eight years, the emperor [Yao] died. The people mourned as for a father or mother for three years, and within the four seas, the eight kinds of music were silenced.
On the first day of the first month, Shun went to the temple of the Ancestor of Culture, consulted with the four mountain chiefs, opened the four gates, clarified the four eyes, and extended the four ears of hearing. "Alas! You twelve shepherds!" he said, "Food is the first necessity! Be gentle with the distant and kind to the near; honor virtue and trust the good; and reject the crafty—then the barbarian tribes will submit."
Shun said, "Alas! You four mountain chiefs! Is there anyone who can vigorously promote the achievements of the emperor, to occupy the general administration and assist in enlightening affairs, and benefit the people?" All said, "Bo Yu is qualified to be Minister of Works." The emperor said, "Yes! Alas! Yu, you have pacified the waters and the soil. Now exert yourself in this work!" Yu bowed and knocked his head, yielding to Ji, Xie, and Gao Yao. The emperor said, "Yes, go and do your work!"
The emperor said, "Qi, the black-haired people are suffering from hunger. Do you, as Minister of Agriculture, sow the various grains in season."
The emperor said, "Xie, the people are not affectionate, and the five relationships are not properly ordered. Do you, as Minister of Education, reverently set forth the five teachings, and be lenient in doing so."
The emperor said, "Gao Yao, the barbarian tribes disturb our land, and robbers and murderers commit crimes. Do you, as Minister of Justice, apply the five punishments; for the five punishments there are three places of execution; for the five banishments there are three places of exile. Only by being clear-sighted can you be trustworthy!"
The emperor said, "Who can manage my various craftsmen?" All said, "Chui!" The emperor said, "Yes! Alas! Chui, you shall be Minister of Works." Chui bowed and knocked his head, yielding to Shu, Qiang, and Bo Yu. The emperor said, "Yes, go! You are the right person."
The emperor said, "Who can manage the plants, trees, birds, and beasts on my hills and in my marshes?" All said, "Yi!" The emperor said, "Yes! Alas! Yi, you shall be my Forester." Yi bowed and knocked his head, yielding to Zhu Hu and Xiong Pi. The emperor said, "Yes, go! You are the right person."
The emperor said, "Alas! You four mountain chiefs, is there anyone who can preside over my three rituals?" All said, "Bo Yi!" The emperor said, "Yes! Alas! Bo, you shall be Master of Ceremonies. Morning and night be reverent; be upright and pure." Bo bowed and knocked his head, yielding to Kui and Long. The emperor said, "Yes, go. Be reverent!"
The emperor said, "Kui! I appoint you to direct music, to teach the young heirs. Be straightforward yet gentle, magnanimous yet stern, firm yet not cruel, simple yet not arrogant. Poetry expresses intent; song prolongs the utterance; the tones follow the prolongation; and the pitch pipes harmonize the tones. When the eight kinds of sounds are in harmony, and none usurps another's place, then spirits and humans are brought into harmony." Kui said, "Ah! I strike the stone and tap the stone, and all the beasts lead one another in dancing."
The emperor said, "Long, I detest slanderous speech and destructive conduct, which shock and alarm my people. I appoint you to be Receiver of Reports, to transmit my commands morning and night, and to be faithful!"
The emperor said, "Alas! You twenty-two men, be reverent! In due season assist in the accomplishments of Heaven." Every three years there was an examination of merits; after three examinations, the worthy were promoted and the unworthy degraded. Thus all achievements flourished. And the San Miao were separated and dealt with.
Shun was summoned at thirty, employed for thirty years, and reigned for fifty years. He died while on a tour of inspection.

zh:
【孔子闲居第二十九】

孔子闲居，子夏侍。子夏曰：“敢问《诗》云：‘凯弟君子，民之父母’，何如斯可谓民之父母矣？”孔子曰：“夫民之父母乎，必达于礼乐之原，以致五至，而行三无，以横于天下。四方有败，必先知之。此之谓民之父母矣。”
子夏曰：“民之父母，既得而闻之矣；敢问何谓‘五至’？”孔子曰：“志之所至，诗亦至焉。诗之所至，礼亦至焉。礼之所至，乐亦至焉。乐之所至，哀亦至焉。哀乐相生。是故，正明目而视之，不可得而见也；倾耳而听之，不可得而闻也；志气塞乎天地，此之谓五至。”
子夏曰：“五至既得而闻之矣，敢问何谓三无？”孔子曰：“无声之乐，无体之礼，无服之丧，此之谓三无。”子夏曰：“三无既得略而闻之矣，敢问何诗近之？”孔子曰：“‘夙夜其命宥密’，无声之乐也。‘威仪逮逮，不可选也’，无体之礼也。‘凡民有丧，匍匐救之’，无服之丧也。”
子夏曰：“言则大矣！美矣！盛矣！言尽于此而已乎？”孔子曰：“何为其然也！君子之服之也，犹有五起焉。”子夏曰：“何如？”子曰：“无声之乐，气志不违；无体之礼，威仪迟迟；无服之丧，内恕孔悲。无声之乐，气志既得；无体之礼，威仪翼翼；无服之丧，施及四国。无声之乐，气志既从；无体之礼，上下和同；无服之丧，以畜万邦。无声之乐，日闻四方；无体之礼，日就月将；无服之丧，纯德孔明。无声之乐，气志既起；无体之礼，施及四海；无服之丧，施于孙子。”

en:
【Confucius at Home at Leisure, Chapter 29】

Confucius was at home at leisure, and Zixia was attending upon him. Zixia said, "May I ask what the Odes mean by 'The gentle and kind gentleman is the parent of the people'? How can one be called the parent of the people?" Confucius said, "Indeed, to be the parent of the people, one must penetrate to the source of rites and music, thereby achieving the Five Extremes and practicing the Three Absences, so as to spread throughout the world. If there is calamity in any of the four directions, one must know of it beforehand. This is what is called being the parent of the people."
Zixia said, "I have heard about being the parent of the people; may I ask what is meant by the 'Five Extremes'?" Confucius said, "Where the will reaches, poetry reaches also. Where poetry reaches, rites reach also. Where rites reach, music reaches also. Where music reaches, sorrow reaches also. Sorrow and joy give birth to each other. Therefore, though one looks with clear eyes, one cannot see it; though one listens with inclined ears, one cannot hear it; yet the will and spirit fill heaven and earth. This is what is called the Five Extremes."
Zixia said, "I have heard about the Five Extremes; may I ask what is meant by the Three Absences?" Confucius said, "Music without sound, rites without form, and mourning without garments—these are called the Three Absences." Zixia said, "I have heard roughly about the Three Absences; may I ask which odes come closest to them?" Confucius said, "'Day and night he maintains his mandate with deep reverence'—this is music without sound. 'His dignified demeanor is graceful, beyond selection'—this is rites without form. 'When the common people have mourning, he hastens to rescue them'—this is mourning without garments."
Zixia said, "The words are great indeed! Beautiful! Abundant! Is that all there is to say?" Confucius said, "How could it be so? When the gentleman puts them into practice, there are still five developments." Zixia said, "What are they?" The Master said, "Music without sound—the will and spirit do not go against; rites without form—the dignified demeanor is leisurely; mourning without garments—inner compassion is deeply sorrowful. Music without sound—the will and spirit are already attained; rites without form—the dignified demeanor is reverent and careful; mourning without garments—it extends to the four states. Music without sound—the will and spirit are already followed; rites without form—the superior and inferior are in harmony; mourning without garments—it nourishes all nations. Music without sound—it is heard daily in the four directions; rites without form—it advances day by day and month by month; mourning without garments—pure virtue is most bright. Music without sound—the will and spirit are already aroused; rites without form—it extends to the four seas; mourning without garments—it extends to descendants."

To the Venerable Master,
I humbly extend my highest respects and hope this letter finds you well.

The memory of that tragedy in the desolate village still weighs heavily upon me, and my chronic ailment shows little sign of abating. Pray, do take great care of yourself. Words cannot capture all I feel; please forgive this humble letter.
With profound respect and unwavering devotion,
Your humble disciple,
Ying

You bow solemnly, just as Uncle Jiang asked of you many years ago. You witnessed that story unfold across Qinghe, and unknowingly became a part of it yourself. The general fighting to the death in blood-stained armor; this is loyalty. The warrior casting aside his name and riding north in disguise; this is righteousness. 镇上的人都知道林钊一心考入公门，但那日镇上来的游侠，一眼看出她的刀法不是公门路子。
林钊看了游侠一眼，没否认，把刀插回腰间。
后来几天，林钊巡街时总能在镇上看见那个游侠。游侠在胡老头的摊子上吃糖饼，在蒙学馆和孩子们一起听课，在风筝坊前仰头看那些花花绿绿的风筝。每次碰见林钊，游侠都远远点个头。
他们熟络起来，林钊才知道游侠是个话多的人，从故乡说到他乡，从江湖说到朝堂，仿佛停不下来。林钊听着，想起自己在江湖上的时候。
几年前，她也在江湖上走过。那时候话更少，刀更快，从一个镇到另一个镇，替人押过镖、清过匪、护过落难的孤寡。她以为江湖就是管闲事，管完了就走，不用留名，也不用落脚。
后来她发现，管得了一时，管不了一世。她救过的人，她走了之后照样被欺。她铲过的匪窝，过几个月又冒出新的。
她便不走了，留在涌泉镇做了一名见习捕快。江湖太大，她想找个能站住脚的地方。
en:
Everyone in town knew Lin Zhao was dead set on officially joining the constabulary. But the wanderer who arrived that day saw right through her at a glance: her blade work didn't come from any government training.
Lin Zhao just gave the wanderer a look. Without a word of denial, she slid her sword back into its sheath.
On her patrols over the next few days, Lin Zhao kept bumping into that wanderer, who would munch on sugar cakes at Elder Hu's stall, sit in on classes with the kids at Primary Hall, or stare up at the bright displays outside the kite workshop. Every time their paths crossed, the wanderer would just offer her a polite nod from afar.
As they got to know each other, Lin Zhao realized the wanderer was a complete chatterbox. The traveler talked endlessly, jumping from tales of home to distant lands, and from the gritty martial underworld to the high politics of the imperial court. Listening to the stories, Lin Zhao couldn't help but think back to her own days as a wanderer.
Years ago, she had roamed that same jianghu. Back then, she spoke even less, and her blade was even faster. Drifting from town to town, she had guarded merchant caravans, cleared out bandit camps, and protected the helpless. She used to think that being a vigilante just meant stepping in to right a wrong and then moving on. No need to leave a name, and no need to put down roots.
But eventually, the reality caught up with her: you can save someone for a day, but not for a lifetime. The people she rescued were victimized all over again the minute she left town. The bandit dens she wiped out were replaced by new ones within months.
So, she stopped wandering. She settled down in Wellspring Town and took a job as a trainee constable. The martial world was simply too vast; she just wanted to find a place where she could finally plant her feet and stand her ground.

游侠，见信好。
前两日外出走了走，碰到个山民，便同行了一程。他好奇地问我，天天刀不离手，怎么就不见这刀出鞘呢，我一时说不出个缘由，便没搭话。
后来我想通了，带着这刀，不单是为了紧要关头能拔出来，它悬在腰间，也是给我自己提个醒，该说什么话，办什么事。刀出不出鞘是其次，人别走岔了路才要紧。游侠，你说是不是？
en:
Greetings, Wanderer.
I went for a walk a couple of days ago and bumped into a mountain dweller, so we traveled together for a while. Out of curiosity, he asked me why I keep my blade on me every single day, yet never draw it from its sheath. For a moment, I couldn't explain why, so I didn't answer.
Later, I figured it out. I carry this blade not just so I can draw it in a life-or-death moment. Having it hang at my waist is also a reminder to myself: a reminder of what words to speak and what deeds to do. Whether the blade leaves the sheath is secondary; what matters is that the man wielding it doesn't stray onto the wrong path.
Wanderer, wouldn't you agree?

en: West of West Lake, mountain ridges stretch on, forming twin peaks, North and South, some ten li apart. Clouds rise over the South Peak before the rain, and clear from the North Peak as the sky first mellows—resembling nothing so much as twin peaks piercing the clouds. Upon the North Peak stands Lingyin Temple, where a lofty pagoda was built during the Tianbao era of the Tang, now restored by the Qian clan. The South Peak likewise bears a pagoda, raised by monks of the Wuyue Region to enshrine sacred relics, its Buddhist chants unceasing. From atop either peak, one may behold the lake and hills of Hangzhou in full splendor; and among the mountain's many caves grow fragrant teas—many a traveler, staff in hand, lingers long in search of a cup, loath to depart.

醉松篇

松树湾的王生，嗜酒如命，每每饮醉归家，必会经过一片松树林。
有一夜，王生在林间踉跄走着，忽然听到身后传来沙沙响动。
他回头张望，四下不见一物，唯有自己的影子。他啐了一口，只当是野鼠作祟。
王生继续前行，谁料那窸窣声竟又响了起来，还愈来愈近……
王生顿觉脊背寒凉，醉意已然散了大半，便发足向林外狂奔。

那鬼祟竟穷追不舍，还发出阵阵嬉笑之声，王生惊惧，不敢有怠，连滚带爬冲出林子。
浑然未觉，怀里的酒囊早已掉落，囊破而酒液四溅。
一炷香的工夫，王生便跑出了松林，跌坐在大石头上喘息，他惊魂未定望向身后……
只见月光之下，一似人非物之影，正伏地舔舐酒渍，状甚贪饕，俄而化作青烟，没入松林。

松树湾故老言，昔年有一嗜酒老翁，醉毙林中，其魂魄甚恋杯中物，不肯散去，便附身于古松。
此乃酒松精怪的由来，它虽模样骇人，却从不伤人性命。追逐王生，也只是馋酒罢了。
王生弃囊不顾，反倒遂了它的心愿。
后来，松树湾的百姓夜过松林，总不忘带上酒囊，行至林深处，便倾洒少许于地。
en:
The Tale of the Drunken Pines

Wang Sheng of Pine Bend, a man devoted to drink, often stumbled home through the dense pine forest. One night, amid the towering trees, he heard rustling behind him. Turning, he saw only his shadow under the moonlight and dismissed the sound as a mouse. But the rustling grew louder and closer. A chill ran down his spine, sobering him enough to flee. Behind him, eerie laughter chased him through the woods. In his panic, he dropped his wine pouch. Safely outside, Wang Sheng glanced back to see a shadowy, otherworldly figure licking the spilled wine before dissolving into a wisp of smoke.

Elders say the spirit is that of a drunken man who died in the forest, his soul forever bound to the wine he loved, now dwelling in an ancient pine. Though fearsome in form, it harms no one, and is only driven by its thirst. By leaving his wine behind, Wang Sheng unknowingly granted the spirit's longing.

From then on, travelers crossing the pine forest at night offer a sip of wine to honor the restless spirit within the ancient trees.

几年过去了，铺子不温不火，他也没发什么财。
不过，他似乎明白了当初来富赖着不走，大概是喜欢躲在油纸伞后捉迷藏。
庄鸿铭也想通了：有生意，就安心做伞；没生意，就蹲着陪来富捉迷藏。人这一生，平安快乐就是福。富不富不重要，有福就好。
en:
They say a cat brings poverty and a dog brings wealth. An oil-paper umbrella shop got a dog who just wouldn't leave.
Zhuang Hongming was overjoyed; surely this was a good omen! Business would boom, and he would make a fortune.
Years have passed. Business is steady, but he hasn't gotten rich.
Eventually, he figures it out. Riches probably stays because he likes hiding behind the oil-paper umbrellas.
Zhuang Hongming makes peace with it: when there are customers, he quietly makes umbrellas; when there are none, he crouches down and plays hide-and-seek with Riches.
A peaceful, happy life, that's its own blessing. Rich or not, it doesn't matter. Being blessed is enough.

en:
"Ghost Hand" is what Pei Hang was called within the "Golden Belt."
The words "Golden Belt" refer not to some rich and precious ornament, but to a poisoned blade.
So long as one could meet its price, it would answer to any master, and wherever its edge passed, blood would stain a thousand miles.
But to Pei Hang, blood itself was reward enough.
From his employer, he learned of the Inkbound Order's singular skill in tracing back old cases, and from this, he formed designs of his own.
He claimed to have inherited the martial arts of the last survivor of the inn massacre, and offered up that counterfeit Zhenguan Jade as proof, all so that the Inkbound Order might be led to Yuzhen's whereabouts.

想起当年与你赌约，谁先定凉州之局，让河西齐聚一心，谁便赢了。如今我沦为阶下囚，苟延性命；但你的大旗亦未至凉州，也不能算赢。

en:
To Lord Zhang,

Amid the turmoil within the Uhu, long has it been since I last wrote. Though I maneuver within the wolf's den, I have failed to broker peace between the Tang and the Uhu—a matter of profound regret.

I recall our wager of yesteryear: whoever first stabilized Liangzhou and united Hexi would be the victor. Today, I am a captive, my life hanging by a thread; yet your banners have not reached Liangzhou, so you too have not yet won.

I am now unarmed, with naught but this command hairpin. Within it are hidden the records of my years in this land; upon its surface, my title is engraved as a prayer for a peaceful era. I gift this pin to you. When that prosperous age arrives, and the historians set down their brushes, you must remind them to write of my title.

The world is in chaos; I fear I shall not see the day you win our wager. When the willows are green once more, pluck a branch and cast it into the river. Let it be a message, a boast to me that you have finally won.
